subtopic_detail: A tense tender vulval swelling with fluctuance at the posterior introitus in a woman with a second episode in two years
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department seeing a 28 year old woman with three days of increasing pain at the entrance to the vagina on the right, now so severe that she cannot sit or walk comfortably.

She had a similar swelling on the same side two years ago that was drained with a scalpel incision in this department and recurred within four months. She is otherwise well, uses condoms for contraception and had a negative sexual health screen six months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant swelling of 4 cm at the right posterior introitus displacing the labium laterally, overlying skin erythematous and thinned at one point, marked tenderness on palpation, no surrounding induration extending onto the thigh or perineum, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, cervix healthy on speculum examination with no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, self collected vaginal swab for nucleic acid testing sent for chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange excision of the entire gland under general anaesthesia and send the specimen for histological examination
options.rationale: Gland excision carries risks of significant bleeding from the underlying vestibular bulb, scarring and dyspareunia, and it is reserved for repeated recurrence after lesser procedures or when malignancy is suspected. Malignancy is considered particularly in women over forty with a solid or irregular mass. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Incise and drain the abscess under local anaesthesia and pack the cavity with ribbon gauze for removal in 48 hours
options.rationale: Simple incision with packing relieves pain but the tract closes over as it heals, which is why recurrence approaches one in three and why this woman is back with a second episode on the same side. It remains acceptable where a catheter is unavailable. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for seven days and arrange outpatient review at the end of the course
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not resolve a tense fluctuant collection, which needs drainage, and they are added only when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic sepsis, pregnancy or immunosuppression. Relying on them here prolongs severe pain and risks spontaneous rupture with an unstructured tract. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Arrange marsupialisation of the gland on the next elective theatre list and manage her pain with oral analgesia meanwhile
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is an effective definitive option but requires theatre and usually regional or general anaesthesia, and making her wait with a tense abscess is not acceptable. It is generally reserved for recurrence after catheter drainage. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

options.text: Incise the abscess under local anaesthesia and insert a balloon tipped catheter to be left in place for four weeks
options.rationale: Insertion of a balloon tipped catheter after incision creates a permanent epithelialised drainage tract and reduces recurrence to roughly five to fifteen per cent, compared with about a third after simple incision and drainage, which is the pattern she has already experienced. The procedure is performed under local anaesthesia and the catheter remains for four to six weeks while the tract epithelialises. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses

explanation.summary: A Bartholin abscess forms when the duct of the greater vestibular gland obstructs and the retained secretion becomes infected, typically with mixed vaginal and enteric flora rather than with a sexually transmissible organism, although testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is still offered. The key management principle is that drainage must create a tract that stays open, because a cavity that simply collapses and heals recurs in around a third of women. Insertion of a balloon tipped catheter through a small incision, left in place for four to six weeks, allows the tract to epithelialise and reduces recurrence substantially while being performed under local anaesthesia in the emergency department or clinic. Antibiotics are added for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression rather than routinely. In women over forty, and in any woman with a solid, fixed or irregular mass, biopsy or excision is considered because carcinoma of the gland, though rare, presents in this way.
key_points: Drainage that leaves a patent epithelialised tract is what prevents recurrence, not the drainage itself.
Balloon catheter insertion reduces recurrence to roughly five to fifteen per cent compared with about a third after simple incision.
Antibiotics are adjunctive and indicated for cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression.
Marsupialisation and gland excision are reserved for recurrence after catheter drainage.
A solid or irregular vulval mass, particularly over the age of forty, prompts biopsy for carcinoma.
explanation.pearls: Place the incision on the mucosal surface just outside the hymenal ring rather than on the skin of the labium, because a tract that opens into the vestibule drains along the gland's natural course and a skin incision tends to produce a scarred, poorly draining channel.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Management of Bartholin gland cysts and abscesses
BMJ Best Practice: Bartholin cyst and abscess

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with vomiting at twenty six weeks where ultrasound of the appendix is non diagnostic
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar asked by the surgical team to review a 30 year old woman at 26 weeks gestation who has had 18 hours of central abdominal pain that has moved to the right side, with nausea and two vomits and no appetite.

She has had no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms and no vaginal loss, and she reports normal foetal movements. She has had no previous abdominal surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 152 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness with guarding in the right flank at the level of the umbilicus, pain worse when she lies on her left side, uterus soft and non tender with no palpable contractions, no renal angle tenderness, cardiotocograph with normal baseline variability and no decelerations, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (5.5 to 15.0 in pregnancy) with neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine with no organisms and no pyuria, lipase within normal limits, transabdominal ultrasound reporting the appendix as not visualised with no free fluid and a normal right kidney

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen without gadolinium contrast, to be reported urgently by the radiologist
options.rationale: When ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix in pregnancy, magnetic resonance imaging is the next investigation because it has high sensitivity and specificity for appendicitis, involves no ionising radiation and reliably identifies alternative diagnoses. Gadolinium is omitted as it crosses the placenta and is avoided unless the benefit is compelling. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids and observation with serial examination and repeat inflammatory markers in 12 hours
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable when the clinical probability is low, but she has migratory pain, localised guarding, fever and a neutrophilia, and perforation risk rises sharply with each hour of delay in pregnancy. Foetal loss after perforated appendicitis is several times that of uncomplicated appendicitis, so the diagnostic pathway is accelerated rather than paused. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics and plan non operative management with a repeat ultrasound scan in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotic only management of appendicitis has a high failure rate and is not the standard approach in pregnancy, where perforation threatens the pregnancy as well as the woman. Repeating a scan that has already failed to see the appendix is unlikely to change the picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast and abdominal shielding applied
options.rationale: Computed tomography is accurate and is used when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or the woman is too unstable to lie still for it, but it delivers foetal radiation exposure that is avoidable when a comparable test exists. Shielding does not meaningfully reduce the internal scatter dose to the uterus. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

options.text: Give intramuscular betamethasone and arrange transfer to a tertiary centre before any further imaging is undertaken
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is given when preterm birth is anticipated within seven days, and she has no uterine activity or cervical change, so it does not take precedence over establishing the diagnosis. If surgery is required, steroid cover and transfer can be arranged in parallel rather than instead of imaging. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Antenatal corticosteroids

explanation.summary: Appendicitis is the commonest non obstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy and is harder to diagnose because the appendix is displaced upward and laterally by the growing uterus, nausea and leucocytosis are physiological, and abdominal guarding is blunted by a lax anterior wall. Ultrasound is the appropriate first imaging test, being safe and often diagnostic, but the appendix is frequently not visualised beyond the first trimester. Magnetic resonance imaging is then the investigation of choice, with sensitivity and specificity above ninety per cent, no ionising radiation and the additional benefit of identifying alternative causes such as ovarian torsion, degenerating fibroid, pyelonephritis and biliary disease. Delay is the main driver of harm: perforation raises foetal loss rates several fold and increases preterm birth, so the diagnostic pathway is compressed rather than extended. Laparoscopic appendicectomy is safe in experienced hands through all trimesters, and management is multidisciplinary with obstetric input on foetal monitoring, thromboprophylaxis and corticosteroid cover if preterm birth becomes likely.
key_points: The appendix shifts upward and laterally with advancing gestation, so pain localises above and lateral to the usual point.
Leucocytosis is physiological in pregnancy, which reduces the value of the white cell count in isolation.
Ultrasound is the first imaging test, and non visualisation of the appendix is common after the first trimester.
Magnetic resonance imaging without gadolinium is the next test and also identifies alternative diagnoses.
Perforation substantially increases foetal loss and preterm birth, so diagnostic delay is the principal hazard.
explanation.pearls: A neutrophil count above about 80 per cent of the total white cell count is far more discriminating than the absolute white cell count in pregnancy, because the physiological leucocytosis of pregnancy does not usually produce that degree of left shift.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Diagnostic imaging in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Continuous urinary leakage beginning three days after a prolonged obstructed labour with a stillbirth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional hospital seeing a 24 year old woman who arrived in Australia two years ago. She gave birth three weeks ago overseas while visiting family, after three days in labour in a village with no operating theatre, and her baby was stillborn.

Since the fourth day after the birth she has leaked urine continuously, day and night, and now wears folded cloth. She is dry between episodes of nothing, describes no urge before leakage, and has developed a rash on the inner thighs. She has no fever and her lochia stopped a week ago.

data_table.Examination: Ammoniacal odour with continuous clear fluid pooling in the vagina on speculum examination, an area of loss of tissue of about 1 cm in the anterior vaginal wall just below the bladder neck with surrounding induration, excoriated erythematous skin over both inner thighs, uterus involuted and non tender, no abdominal distension or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 74 micromol/L (45 to 90), midstream urine with mixed growth and pyuria, dye test with methylene blue instilled into the bladder showing blue staining of the vaginal swab

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer her for immediate surgical repair of the defect on the next available gynaecology operating list this week
options.rationale: Operating into inflamed, oedematous and partly necrotic tissue in the first weeks after an obstructed labour fistula gives a high rate of breakdown, and repair is conventionally deferred until the tissues are healthy, generally around three months after the injury. Continuous drainage in the meantime is what maximises the chance of spontaneous closure and of a successful later repair. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for continuous bladder drainage and refer her to a urogynaecology service
options.rationale: Continuous bladder drainage keeps the bladder empty so that the fistulous tract has the best chance of closing spontaneously, which occurs in a meaningful proportion of small fresh fistulas, and it immediately stops the skin damage and the social consequences of constant leakage. Specialist referral then plans nutritional support, skin care and definitive repair when the tissues have healed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Commence anticholinergic therapy for detrusor overactivity and arrange formal urodynamic studies in the coming weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat urgency incontinence, in which leakage follows an urge and the woman is dry between episodes, whereas she leaks continuously without urge and blue dye has already passed into the vagina. Urodynamics has no role once a fistula is demonstrated. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

options.text: Prescribe oral trimethoprim for seven days and review her once the urinary tract infection has been fully treated
options.rationale: Pyuria and mixed growth are expected when urine pools in the vagina and the perineum is constantly wet, so treating the culture result does not address the cause and delays definitive care. Antibiotics are given for symptomatic infection alongside drainage rather than in place of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Refer her for pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist and review her progress in three months
options.rationale: Pelvic floor training is the first line treatment for stress incontinence, where leakage accompanies coughing or exertion and the pelvic floor is intact, and it cannot close an epithelialised communication between bladder and vagina. Offering it here would leave her leaking for another three months. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

explanation.summary: Obstetric vesicovaginal fistula is caused by pressure necrosis of the bladder base and anterior vaginal wall trapped between the foetal head and the pubic symphysis during prolonged obstructed labour, and it is rare where caesarean section is accessible but remains a major cause of morbidity worldwide. The presentation is continuous painless leakage of urine beginning a few days after the birth, usually after a labour that ended in stillbirth, and the associated injuries may include foot drop from lumbosacral plexus compression, vaginal stenosis and secondary amenorrhoea. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a dye test in which methylene blue instilled into the bladder stains a vaginal swab, and by imaging or examination under anaesthesia to define the site and size and to exclude a ureteric fistula, in which the dye test is negative. Early management is continuous catheter drainage, which allows some small fresh fistulas to close spontaneously, together with skin barrier care, nutrition and treatment of infection. Definitive repair is undertaken by an experienced surgeon once inflammation has settled, and women need psychological and social support because the condition frequently brings isolation and stigma.
key_points: Continuous painless leakage starting days after a prolonged obstructed labour is the hallmark presentation.
A positive dye test localises the leak to the bladder; a negative test with ongoing leakage suggests a ureteric fistula.
Continuous catheter drainage is the immediate treatment and allows some fresh fistulas to close without surgery.
Repair is deferred until the tissues are healthy, conventionally around three months after injury.
Associated injuries include foot drop, vaginal stenosis and amenorrhoea, and psychosocial support is integral.
explanation.pearls: If the dye test is negative but leakage continues, the next step is a three swab test with intravenous indigo carmine or contrast imaging, because a ureterovaginal fistula leaks urine that never enters the bladder and will therefore never stain blue.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric fistula

subtopic_detail: Planning intrapartum care at booking for a woman with type three female genital cutting in her first pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a booking visit for a 26 year old woman at 13 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy, who came to Australia as a child. Through a professional interpreter she says she was cut as a girl in her country of birth and that passing urine takes several minutes.

She has intercourse with difficulty and has never had a cervical screening test. She asks what will happen when the baby is born and says her mother expects her to be closed again afterwards.

data_table.Examination: Fused labial tissue forming a horizontal bridge across the introitus with a posterior opening of approximately 8 mm, clitoral tissue not visible, no vulval ulceration or discharge, no inclusion cyst palpable, abdominal examination consistent with 13 weeks gestation
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods unremarkable with haemoglobin 118 g/L (110 to 140), dating ultrasound consistent with 13 weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her care?

options.text: Book an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the safest mode of birth and counsel her accordingly at this visit
options.rationale: Female genital cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean section, and recommending surgery to avoid addressing the infibulation exposes her to operative risk and to the same problem in future pregnancies. Mode of birth is decided on the usual obstetric grounds after deinfibulation has been arranged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Plan deinfibulation in the first stage of labour under epidural analgesia, with no antenatal genital procedure offered
options.rationale: Deinfibulation during labour is an acceptable fallback when a woman declines the antenatal procedure or presents late, but it is performed under time pressure by whoever is on duty and removes the opportunity for unhurried consent and healing. Offering only this option narrows her choices without clinical justification. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Offer antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester and document that reinfibulation will not be performed after the birth
options.rationale: Antenatal deinfibulation, usually offered around the second trimester, allows vaginal examination, catheterisation and birth without an emergency procedure and gives the woman time to recover and to adjust before labour. Reinfibulation is unlawful throughout Australia and this is explained clearly and non judgementally to the woman at the same consultation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Make a mandatory report to the state child protection service about the procedure she underwent as a child overseas
options.rationale: Reporting obligations attach to a child currently at risk, so the trigger would be a daughter or another girl in the family who might be cut, not the historical cutting of an adult patient. Reporting an adult woman for her own childhood experience breaches her confidence and deters women from seeking maternity care. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

options.text: Defer any genital examination or discussion until 36 weeks so that she can settle into antenatal care with her midwife
options.rationale: Delaying the conversation to 36 weeks leaves no time for an antenatal procedure, for urological assessment of her voiding difficulty, or for interpreter supported discussion of her preferences. Early identification is the step that opens every subsequent option. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting

explanation.summary: Female genital cutting is classified by the World Health Organization into four types, of which type three, infibulation, involves narrowing of the vaginal opening by creating a covering seal and is the type that causes obstructed voiding, dyspareunia, recurrent infection and difficulty with intrapartum examination and birth. Australian maternity care identifies affected women early, ideally at booking, using a professional interpreter rather than a family member, and offers deinfibulation antenatally, usually in the second trimester, so that the procedure is unhurried and healed before labour. Intrapartum deinfibulation remains available for women who decline or who present late. Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions and this is explained respectfully rather than punitively, acknowledging family expectations while being clear about the legal position. Child protection obligations relate to girls currently at risk, so the relevant question is whether any daughter or other child in the family may be taken overseas for cutting, and the woman herself is a patient rather than a subject of reporting.
key_points: Type three cutting narrows the introitus and causes voiding difficulty, dyspareunia and intrapartum obstruction.
Antenatal deinfibulation, usually in the second trimester, is offered so the procedure is planned rather than emergent.
Cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean section.
Reinfibulation after birth is unlawful in Australia and is discussed openly and without judgement.
Mandatory reporting concerns girls at current risk, not the adult woman's own history.
explanation.pearls: A professional interpreter who is not a family member is a clinical requirement rather than a courtesy in these consultations, because disclosure of cutting, of its type, and of family pressure for reinfibulation is unlikely when a relative is interpreting.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Female genital mutilation or cutting
World Health Organization: Care of girls and women living with female genital mutilation
